quotes.text: Akira Ifukube's scores for Nikkatsu are some of his finest film works, from the heartwarming score to "The Maid's Child", the Jazz-like score to "Scoundrels of the Sea", to the emotional score to "The Burmese Harp".
Ifukube and Hayasaka would form the core of a group of nationalistic composers - "nationalistic" in the sense that they tried to develop a Japanese music tradition different from the European one.

Ifukube was the first composer to use Japanese folk music in compositions based on European techniques. In this first work there is an extensive use of ostinati (short motives repeated over and over again), a technique that would characterize all Ifukube's work.

Ifukube used a scale that was basically pentatonic, to which he would add one or two notes not used by the melody. To create a harmonic texture he would often use double musical lines, simple counterpoint or canonic sections.

There is an interesting contrast between the graceful folk tunes and the "Aboriginal" quality called up by the ostinati, the doubling of the melody and the use of open fifths in the harmony. The music is very rhythmic, with a prominent place for the percussion section.
The work is written in a naive style and combines the energy of folk music with the structural and instrumental patterns of European music.

His compositional efforts drew from Japanese folk traditions, Ainu chants encountered in Hokkaido, and European modernist influences, reflecting a deliberate fusion of ethnic and symphonic elements without formal instruction.

This period marked his transition from amateur sketches to structured works, underscoring his status as a self-educated composer in an era when formal conservatory paths dominated Japanese musical development.

His initial compositions emerged in the early 1930s, beginning with Three Songs of Autumn from the Heian Period (1932) for mezzo-soprano and piano, his earliest documented attempt integrating ancient Japanese poetic forms with modern harmony.

His first published piece, Piano Suite (1933), for solo piano, comprised four movements—"Bon-Odori," "Tanabata," "Ensei," and a second "Tanabata"—evoking rural festivals and seasonal motifs through rhythmic vitality and modal structures derived from folk sources.

Japanese Rhapsody (1935), his debut orchestral work, earned the prestigious Alexander Tcherepnin Prize in 1936 for its innovative orchestration blending Japanese pentatonic scales with Western symphonic form.
These early efforts established Ifukube's signature approach: robust, primal textures emphasizing percussion and brass to convey elemental forces, prefiguring his later cinematic style.
One of the most respected of serious composers in Japan since the 1950s, Akira Ifukube has also led something of a double life as one of the most popular and prolific film composers in Japan.
